characteristics.harvestSeason: First flush (ichibancha) — late April to May

description.short: Japan's ubiquitous steamed green tea — crisp, briskly refreshing, with pronounced oceanic umami from brief steam fixation
description.overview: The cornerstone of everyday Japanese tea culture, representing the vast majority of the nation's harvest. Its defining technical trait is steam fixation rather than pan-firing in a wok as done in China.
description.leaf: Slender, glossy dark green pine-needle-like rolled leaves
description.aroma: Fresh, marine, lightly grassy with sweet seaweed notes
description.taste: Vibrant, rich umami sweetness, gentle astringency, and crisp refreshing vegetable notes
description.processing: Plucking → hot steam fixation (15–20 seconds, unlike pan-firing) → rolling and needle shaping → drying

history.origin: Steam fixation technology arrived in Japan from Tang-era China, but while China later abandoned steaming in favor of dry pan-firing, Japan perfected steam crafting into its national standard.
history.development: Modern sencha took form in the 18th century when master Nagatani Soen revolutionized rolling and drying methods (the Uji method) to create beautiful needle leaves.
history.modern: Today Sencha is the quintessential daily tea of Japan, consumed throughout homes, restaurants, and offices in contrast to ceremonial matcha.
interestingFacts: Retaining steam fixation rather than pan-roasting is the primary technological divide separating Japanese green teas from Chinese green teas.
Master Nagatani Soen, who refined sencha crafting in 1738, is revered across Japan as the father of modern Japanese green tea.
